title: Blue bubble in Carina
caption: The Wolf-Rayet star WR 31a and its blue bubble, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: WR 31a · constellation Carina · about 30000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A distinctive blue bubble seems to surround a sparkling star at the center of this Hubble image. The star is WR 31a, a Wolf-Rayet star about 30,000 light-years away in Carina, the Keel, and it has an uncataloged companion. The bubble is a Wolf-Rayet nebula, a cloud of dust, hydrogen, helium and other gases.

Such nebulae form when fast stellar winds collide with the outer layers of hydrogen that Wolf-Rayet stars have thrown off, and they are often ring-shaped or spherical. This bubble is thought to be around 20 000 years old, and it is growing at around 220 000 kilometers per hour.

Wolf-Rayet stars do not last long, just a few hundred thousand years, a brief moment in astronomical terms. They start out with at least 20 times the Sun's mass but typically lose half of it in under 100 000 years. WR 31a will eventually explode as a supernova, and its scattered material will later feed new stars and planets.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.63 x 1.57 arcminutes) and distance (30000 light years), the frame spans roughly 14 × 14 light-years. Its light set out about 30,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the star through a visible and a near-infrared filter. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, so part of this picture records light we could never see directly.
